interest: This file provides a fascinating glimpse into U.S.-China wartime technical collaboration during World War II, specifically the Cultural Relations program's deployment of American agricultural scientists to enhance domestic food security and crop yields in unoccupied China. It highlights the sharp bureaucratic and logistical friction between civilian agricultural assistance and urgent military airlift priorities over the Hump, illustrated by the Embassy's hesitation to allocate air cargo capacity for seed potatoes. Furthermore, the documents serve as an instructive example of State Department recordkeeping anomalies, as materials relating entirely to Republic of China affairs (893.61a) were misfiled under the decimal file for Japan (894.61A).
overview: This file consists of two incoming telegrams received in 1943 from the U.S. Embassy in Chungking (Chongqing), China, addressed to the Secretary of State in Washington. Although classified under decimal file 894.61A—nominally designating internal affairs of Japan concerning agricultural advisers—the documents relate entirely to wartime agricultural aid and advisory missions in China under the Department of State's Cultural Relations program, having been marked with China decimal 893.61a before being filed under 894.61A. The first telegram conveys an urgent request by plant pathologist Dr. Theodore Dykstra for the air shipment of foundation seed potatoes from Beltsville, Maryland, to boost Chinese crop production, alongside the Embassy's caveat regarding strict military airlift priorities. The second telegram, sent by Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss, reports that agricultural specialist Phillips plans to conclude his mission by January 1, 1944, and return to Washington despite the Chinese Ministry of Agriculture's request for an extension.

subfiles.about: Dr. Theodore Dykstra requests air shipment of foundation seed potatoes from the United States to China to improve domestic food yields, while the Embassy notes competing military transport priorities.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Theodore Dykstra, serving in China under the Cultural Relations program, requests that a cable be transmitted to Dr. F. Stevenson of the Potato Project at the Bureau of Plant Industry in Beltsville, Maryland, ordering foundation seed and tubers of diverse American potato varieties for shipment to China. Dykstra asserts that improved seed selection and disease control can double or triple Chinese potato yields, making it an essential food crop, but insists the potatoes must arrive by plane before January 1 to avoid rotting during uncooled sea transit. In forwarding the message, Chargé d'Affaires George Atcheson, Jr. informs the Department that while recognizing the immense value of Dykstra's program, the Embassy cannot definitively recommend air transport given the critical urgency of military cargo.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Chargé Atcheson (Chungking) on Seed Potato Request by Dr. Theodore Dykstra

subfiles.about: Ambassador Gauss reports that agricultural specialist Phillips plans to conclude his assignment in China by January 1, 1944, and return to Washington.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss advises the Secretary of State that agricultural adviser Phillips intends to finish his mission in China by January 1, 1944, and depart shortly thereafter. Although the Chinese Ministry of Agriculture requested that Phillips extend his stay, Phillips decided that an extension was inadvisable following a request from McPhee. Gauss notes that Phillips is awaiting telegraphic routing instructions for his return journey to Washington as previously requested by the Embassy.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Ambassador Gauss (Chungking) on Departure Plans of Agricultural Adviser Phillips
